Boston’s metropolitan real estate investment market in 2024 is best characterized as supply-constrained, economically resilient, and structurally “high-demand/high-cost,” with pricing and rents supported by durable fundamentals even as elevated interest rates compress transaction volume. The region’s long-run housing scarcity reflects decades of restrictive land-use regulation and limited new supply relative to job growth—conditions repeatedly linked in the academic literature to higher prices and greater price stickiness in regulated metros (Glaeser, Gyourko, & Saks, 2005; Saiz, 2010). In 2024, these structural constraints intersect with a post-pandemic reset in space use: office demand remains weaker and more polarized by building quality, while multi-family and “workforce” rental demand remains underpinned by a large student/early-career population, tight vacancy, and the metro’s high-income, innovation-driven labor base. Research on Boston’s agglomeration economy and skill clustering helps explain why demand tends to re-form even after shocks, as high-skill labor markets and knowledge spillovers support persistent willingness to pay for proximity (Glaeser & Maré, 2001). A notable pattern in 2024 is the widening bifurcation between assets benefiting from scarcity (well-located housing, transit-oriented rentals, and specialized life-science-adjacent product) and assets facing secular headwinds (commodity suburban office), consistent with evidence that real estate cycles transmit differently across property types depending on local supply elasticities and demand shocks (Gyourko, Mayer, & Sinai, 2013).

From an investment-opportunity standpoint, the strongest risk-adjusted plays in 2024 skew toward (1) multi-family acquisitions or development in transit-served submarkets where entitlement risk is manageable and tenant demand is deep, because constrained supply and inelastic land availability tend to stabilize cash flows and support rent growth over time (Saiz, 2010); (2) value-add “workforce housing” repositioning—smaller multifamily and mixed-use properties in inner-ring communities—where operational improvements can capture rent premiums without relying on aggressive macro appreciation, an approach aligned with how tight supply environments reward incremental quality upgrades; and (3) selective office-to-residential conversion or adaptive reuse in locations with strong amenities and transit, given the persistence of housing shortages and the emerging discount to older office stock (while recognizing that only a subset of buildings are physically and financially convertible). Finally, niche opportunities may exist in assets tied to Boston’s research and medical ecosystem (e.g., housing near major employment nodes), reflecting the broader finding that human-capital-intensive metros exhibit durable demand linked to productivity and wages (Glaeser & Maré, 2001). Overall, the 2024 pattern is “low volume, high selectivity”: tighter financing conditions raise the bar for leverage and underwriting, but Boston’s long-term price support—rooted in regulation- and geography-driven scarcity—continues to favor investors who can access well-located housing exposure, execute operational improvements, or repurpose obsolete space into residential supply (Glaeser et al., 2005; Gyourko et al., 2013; Saiz, 2010; Glaeser & Maré, 2001; DiPasquale & Wheaton, 1992).

- Glaeser, E. L., & Maré, D. C. (2001). Cities and skills. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 19(2), 316–342.  
- Gyourko, J., Mayer, C., & Sinai, T. (2013). Superstar cities. *American Economic Journal: Economic Policy*, 5(4), 167–199.  
- Saiz, A. (2010). The geographic determinants of housing supply. *The Quarterly Journal of Economics*, 125(3), 1253–1296.
